flashcards.q: Name the 7 OSI layers in order.
flashcards.a: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

flashcards.q: How does TCP/IP's 4-layer model map to OSI's 7?
flashcards.a: Application (collapses Session+Presentation+Application), Transport (=OSI Transport), Internet (=OSI Network), Link (collapses Physical+Data Link; some texts split this back into 5 layers).

flashcards.q: What is the Ethernet header size, and what's added by an 802.1Q VLAN tag?
flashcards.a: 14 bytes (6B dst MAC + 6B src MAC + 2B EtherType), plus a 4-byte FCS trailer. A VLAN tag adds 4 more bytes (max frame goes from 1518 to 1522).

flashcards.q: What are the minimum IPv4, IPv6, TCP, and UDP header sizes?
flashcards.a: IPv4: 20B (up to 60B with options). IPv6: 40B fixed, no options field. TCP: 20B (up to 60B with options). UDP: 8B flat, always.

flashcards.q: Compute total non-payload overhead for a TCP segment on a 1500-byte-MTU Ethernet link with no options, and the resulting usable payload.
flashcards.a: 14 (Eth) + 20 (IP) + 20 (TCP) + 4 (FCS) = 58 bytes overhead. Usable payload = 1500 - 20 - 20 = 1460 bytes, which is the default MSS on a 1500-MTU path.

flashcards.q: Why did TCP/IP win over OSI's own protocol suite (X.25, CLNP)?
flashcards.a: "Rough consensus and running code" beat design-by-committee: TCP/IP was already deployed and iterating on real networks years before OSI's transport/network protocols were finalized.

flashcards.q: Does the OSI model exist as running protocols today?
flashcards.a: No. It survives purely as shared vocabulary ("layer 3 switch", "layer 7 load balancer") describing devices built on a TCP/IP stack, not as deployed protocols.

flashcards.q: What's the correct diagnostic ladder for "the network is slow"?
flashcards.a: ping (L3 reachability) -> traceroute/mtr (L3 path) -> nc -zv/curl -v (L4 reachability) -> tcpdump (raw bytes) -> application logs (L7) LAST.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between getting an RST vs a silent timeout when connecting to a port?
flashcards.a: RST means the destination actively refused (something's up, but nothing listening on that port) -- fast. A silent timeout means the packet was filtered or the host is unreachable -- slow, no information.

flashcards.q: What is duplex mismatch, and what's its observable symptom?
flashcards.a: One end of an Ethernet link auto-negotiates full-duplex while the other is half-duplex. Symptom: throughput collapses to a fraction of link speed while ethtool -S shows climbing rx_crc_errors / late collisions on the half-duplex side; app logs show only vague intermittent slowness.

flashcards.q: Where does TLS fit in the OSI model, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Functionally it does what OSI called Presentation (encryption/formatting), but it's implemented as a library between the application and the transport socket -- there's no standalone OSI Presentation-layer protocol in a real stack.

flashcards.q: Why don't modern technologies like QUIC or eBPF/XDP map cleanly to one OSI layer?
flashcards.a: QUIC moves transport-layer responsibility (reliability, congestion control) into a user-space library riding over UDP; eBPF/XDP processes packets in the kernel driver context before the normal stack runs. Both deliberately span layer boundaries rather than fitting one box.
